title: Captree and the Bay Islands: Native Agreements and Competing Claims
summary: Secatogue people named in a 1705 beach deed, an English island patent, and rival town claims all belong in this history. The 1814 decree rejected both litigants’ titles to Captree, Oak and Grass; later town agreements did not constitute new Native consent.
address_label: Captree Island — modern coastal context, not a deed survey
map_geometry_source: Modern coastline components compared with USCGS Captree Island Cut survey H05370A (1934). Approximate landscape, not a Native deed, lease parcel or current ownership survey.
why_this_matters: Naming the Native parties and colonial trustees makes responsibility visible. The island lawsuit and later town quitclaim show that paper claims could conflict; they do not prove Native consent, disappearance or the end of relationships with the bay.

history_title: Native parties, colonial property and contested control
history_content:
A homeland across beach and bay

Captree is a low marsh island north of Captree State Park, crossed today by Robert Moses Causeway. It sits within a coastal landscape shaped by Native relationships long before English towns and estates. The National Park Service describes Unkechaug, Secatogue and Shinnecock connections to the neighboring barrier beach and waters, and continuing Native stewardship. This regional account does not identify a particular village on Captree. Native American Heritage at Fire Island National Seashore

Who made the beach agreement?

On October 29, 1705, a deed recorded Secatogue proprietors Wameahus, Charles Pemequa, Rowwo, Mumsuwaren, Mamme, Jo Chepous and Peter in its opening text. The receiving parties were Huntington trustees John Wickes, John Wood, Epenetus Platt, Jonathan Jarves, Richard Brush and John Ketcham. Huntington was then an English colonial town in the Province of New York; its south-shore territory included places now in Babylon. Spellings vary within the record. The acknowledgment names Wameahus, Charles Pamequa, Mumsuwaren, Peter and Jo Chepous. Huntington Town Records, Including Babylon, Volume II

What the document claimed—and what it cannot tell us

The deed described a beach between the town’s patent line and an earlier purchase west of Massapequa Gut, with associated marshes and islands not previously purchased. It did not individually name Captree, Oak or Grass. Its English legal language claimed a perpetual estate in fee simple and required defense against other claims. This is concrete evidence of how colonial documents framed land as transferable property. The wording alone cannot establish how every Native party understood the agreement, or turn its broad description into surveyed island boundaries. Huntington Town Records, Including Babylon, Volume II

A patent did not settle every claim

A separate June 4, 1688 English colonial patent to William Nicoll described islands between Huntington Gut and his land at Conetqunt. A descendant later asserted that it included Captree, Oak and Grass. Huntington’s trustees claimed the same islands under town patents. In 1814, Chancellor James Kent examined conflicting testimony about inlet names, storms and channels that had opened or closed. He found that Nicoll’s patent did not reach those three islands. Nicoll v. Trustees, 1 Johns. Ch. 166

Neither claimant received a victory

The decree copied into the town records states that neither Nicoll nor Huntington’s trustees had title to Captree, Oak and Grass in that proceeding, dismisses the bill without costs and directs related suits to stop. The published opinion explains the failed Nicoll claim and discusses Huntington’s deficient claim while deciding costs. Neither document records a new Native cession or awards the islands back to Native people. The town compilation’s heading says April 29, but the decree itself and reported opinion give August 29, 1814. Huntington Town Records, Including Babylon, Volume III

How town government continued to arrange control

On July 13, 1818, an Islip committee—Nathaniel Conklin, Jonathan Thompson, Jesse Smith and Joshua Willets in the deed’s opening—quitclaimed island and beach interests to Huntington’s trustees for $1,000. The receiving trustees were Timothy Conklin, Thomas Carll, Divine Hewlett, Gilbert Platt, Solomon Ketcham and Samuel Carll. The boundary description follows Brood Creek on Captree to its first forks, then runs south to the Atlantic, alongside the confirmation-patent line. This was an agreement between towns within the state property system, not another agreement with Native people. The published signature list differs in naming Platt Conklin; the later acknowledgment again names Nathaniel. Huntington Town Records, Including Babylon, Volume III

From colonial claims to municipal leases

In 1918, the New York Court of Appeals examined Islip’s power to lease Short Beach in Town of Islip v. Estates of Havemeyer Point. Town electors had authorized leases for buildings in 1855. The disputed 1907 lease offered five years followed by four ten-year renewal options. Islip later sought cancellation. The court treated the land as property the town could manage commercially, reversed the judgment and ordered a new trial. This shows how colonial claims continued through municipal property administration; the case did not decide a Native claim or establish Native consent. Court opinion, 1918, pp. 451–454

A bay landscape leased for business

On December 31, 1952, Islip leased ten acres in eastern Captree to Wa-Wa-Yanda, Inc. for thirty years. The lease authorized a hotel, marina and related activities. A later dispute over zoning reached the courts in 1963. These records reveal another layer of control over Native coastal homelands: town government acting as landlord and deciding which commercial uses could take place. The lease is evidence of later municipal administration, not a Native land sale. Wa-Wa-Yanda court opinion, 1963

Channels changed the shape of the landscape

A federal survey made in May 1934 mapped the Captree marsh complex and a recently dredged channel connecting the State Channel with Fire Island Inlet. Its report described a sand dump on formerly shallow water and a basin dredged after the topography was recorded. The landscape itself was being reshaped as governments and leaseholders controlled its uses. Modern channels divide this historic marsh landscape into several pieces; a present-day outline cannot simply be treated as the boundary of a colonial agreement. Captree Island Cut survey and descriptive report, 1934

Land relationships outlast a paper claim

The record moves from a Native agreement written in English property language to competing patents, litigation and town quitclaims. It does not justify ending Native history at a sale date. Native people continue to care for this coastal region; Poospatuck remains an Unkechaug homeland connected to the bays and Fire Island. Read the neighboring Secatogue and Islip histories for mainland agreements and retained rights, without assuming those clauses apply identically to every island. Native American Heritage at Fire Island National Seashore
whereintheworld_content: This approximate outline follows modern land and marsh components in the Captree landscape, including the causeway crossing and eastern pieces separated by tidal channels. They were compared with the Captree marsh complex on the U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey’s 1934 Captree Island Cut sheet. The map locates the landscape discussed here; it is not the boundary of the 1705 beach deed, the 1688 patent, the 1818 quitclaim or the ten-acre 1952 lease. The court’s approximate 600-acre figure does not define this modern outline. Dredging, erosion and marsh change mean the present shoreline differs from the historic sheet. Oak and Grass appear in the court history but are not individually reconstructed here. This interpretation does not establish current ownership or permission to enter private land. 1934 survey and descriptive report
